one_line: Two creators (Cerebras and OpenAI DevEx) walk through a six-stage AI content pipeline: swipe-file ideation, voice-captured scripts, shot lists, agent-driven editing, captioning, scheduling and a periodic process-review skill.
summary: Sarah Chieng (Cerebras) and Cova Lee (OpenAI) run a workshop on building an AI-assisted video content system organized around six stages: ideating, scripting, recording, editing, repurposing and publishing. Most examples are ChatGPT/Codex prompts and reusable "skills" that encode each creator's voice, research tools, shot lists and editing workflows. Ideation rests on a swipe file of references and on outlier analysis of engagement relative to a channel's own average. Editing is handled by agents driving APIs (HyperFrames) or desktop apps (CapCut, Premiere) rather than manual timelines. The speakers stress that the creator should stay in control, with AI removing tedious work, and they close with a periodic "review my process" skill that finds repetitive work to automate. Much of the content is tool-specific and the presenters work for vendors, so the reusable value is the structure rather than the products.

key_ideas.idea: Organize video production as six stages (ideate, script, record, edit, repurpose, publish) and attach an AI workflow to each one.
key_ideas.detail: The whole workshop follows this structure. Each stage gets its own prompts, skills or tools, so the pipeline can be reused and improved stage by stage.

key_ideas.idea: Build a swipe file of references and let the agent read it to learn your taste.
key_ideas.detail: The swipe file can be a website, Notion, Obsidian or a bookmark folder. The point is that agents pick up creative style better from concrete examples than from text descriptions. Review it occasionally to reset taste.

key_ideas.idea: Judge content by outlier performance relative to the channel's own average, not by absolute views.
key_ideas.detail: Compare each post against the creator's historical baseline and look for multi-x outliers. Thumbnail and title innovation tends to show up in those outliers. The speakers also note that copying only top-performing topics leaves you behind, so they use outliers as a source of new frameworks.

key_ideas.idea: Write scripts by speaking the concept aloud and having the model interview you, then generate several scripts and rank them.
key_ideas.detail: Speaking reduces marketing-sounding phrasing. The agent asks follow-up questions to fill gaps. The workflow generates about three script options and scores them against criteria the creator picks, such as engagement or clarity.

key_ideas.idea: Convert the script into a two-pass shot list: annotate A-roll, B-roll and graphics, then generate a filming checklist.
key_ideas.detail: The first pass annotates the script with shot types. The second pass produces a checklist for filming. Screen-recording demos can be found in an always-on local recording of the screen through a tool that integrates with Codex CLI.

key_ideas.idea: Edit with agents that call editing APIs or drive desktop apps, and keep granular control only where you need it.
key_ideas.detail: HyperFrames (HeyGen) produces pre-rendered video that is regenerated on each prompt, which suits prompt-driven edits. Layer-level work needs a real editor. CapCut and Final Cut were the editors where the speakers saw the best agent control, through computer use or MCP.

key_ideas.idea: Build a weekly process-review skill that finds time sinks and repetitive tasks to automate, then update the skills it names.
key_ideas.detail: The skill reviews how time is spent across the pipeline and proposes automations. In the example it found a duplicate triage location and a Premiere import check that cost time on every open, and the creator dropped that check.

key_ideas.idea: Keep the creator in the driver's seat: AI removes tedious steps but the voice, taste and ideas must be the creator's own.
key_ideas.detail: The speakers emphasize that without the creator's judgment the content becomes generic. Captions, rotoscoping and similar tedious work are offloaded. The bigger questions (what to say, what is good) stay human.

techniques.name: Swipe-file reference library for agents
techniques.how: Collect favorite videos, posts, thumbnails and bookmarks in one place (Notion, Obsidian, a website or a folder). Give the agent access to that library and ask it to match your taste. Review and prune it about once a year.
techniques.when: Before ideation and before writing titles, thumbnails or captions, so that output matches a chosen style.

techniques.name: Build a voice skill from your own past content
techniques.how: Feed the agent a few pieces of your published content and ask it to capture how you sound. Save the result as a reusable script skill. Then ask it to produce three script options and rank them by criteria you set, such as engagement or clarity percentages.
techniques.when: When you already have a body of published work and want scripts that sound like you, not generic AI copy.

techniques.name: Voice-first script interview
techniques.how: Explain the concept out loud to the agent (voice mode), then ask it to interview you about gaps, unclear parts and relevance, and to suggest cuts. The speakers' prompt pattern is: write a video about this idea, interview me about it. They summarize the rules as concise and clear.
techniques.when: When drafting technical or educational scripts that tend to drift into marketing language.

techniques.name: Outlier analysis against channel baseline
techniques.how: Pull engagement data for each post through an API (the speakers connected the Twitter API to ChatGPT). Compare each post with the channel's historical average, and flag outliers at multiples such as 1x to 20x. Build a research tool for thumbnails and titles on top of that data. Compare apples to apples by testing caption variants across cut-downs of the same long video.
techniques.when: When deciding which hooks, thumbnails, titles or caption styles to repeat.

techniques.name: Two-pass shot list from a script
techniques.how: Pass 1: annotate the script with A-roll, B-roll, screen recording and graphics. Pass 2: generate a filming checklist from the annotated script. Use a local always-on screen recorder to find past demos when you need to re-record them, and a screenshot/annotation tool for blur and arrows.
techniques.when: For technical or dev-facing videos that rely heavily on demos and screen recordings.

techniques.name: Organize footage before editing
techniques.how: Name and file all assets (A-roll, B-roll, screen recordings, screenshots, sound effects) into a folder structure, then let the agent link media into the editor. The speakers say an agent organizes and names files well when asked.
techniques.when: Before any edit, especially for long-form interviews that will be cut into multiple shorts.

techniques.name: Agent-driven editing via API or desktop control
techniques.how: Give the agent a video-editing API's docs (the speakers used HyperFrames) and ask it to set up the API, stitch angles together, add text and captions, and render. Review and iterate with written feedback. For desktop editors, let the agent control CapCut or Premiere through computer use or MCP. Use a custom sound-pad tool so the agent can insert sound effects on a track.
techniques.when: For short-form edits, captions, text animations and sound design, where the creator is fine giving up some frame-level control.

techniques.name: Brand design system generated from your own videos
techniques.how: Ask the coding agent to study your most recent N videos (the speaker used 50 Instagram posts) and turn the recurring visual style into a Figma document. Alternatively, have the model generate about ten brand and logo variants and pick one.
techniques.when: Before building a slide deck or a recurring visual identity, so that all content shares one style.

techniques.name: Background and visual enhancement with image generation
techniques.how: Mask part of a frame (such as the wall behind you) and prompt the image model to fill it while keeping the subject unchanged. Generate three options and pick one. For floating objects, have an agent drive After Effects to model objects in Blender, export them as GLB and place them over the footage.
techniques.when: When the set is bare and you want a more polished look without re-filming.

techniques.name: Fix mistakes with short inserts
techniques.how: Re-record only the wrong word or date, use an avatar or AI speech correction for the short segment, then cut it in. Keep the rest of the take unchanged.
techniques.when: When a long take is mostly good but has a single wrong fact or word.

techniques.name: Repurposing into short-form cut-downs
techniques.how: From one long interview, use the agent to find the strongest sound bites and generate multiple short clips. Use separate skills for each platform (TikTok, Instagram, YouTube Shorts).
techniques.when: When one long-form piece needs to feed a week or more of short posts.

techniques.name: Scheduling with human approval
techniques.how: Put the finished clips in a folder and ask a scheduling tool to post one clip per day or week on each platform, research the best posting times, and draft captions for your approval before anything goes live.
techniques.when: When you want a steady cadence across several channels without writing every caption by hand.

techniques.name: Remove AI tells from captions and prose
techniques.how: Paste the Wikipedia article "Signs of AI Writing" into the prompt and instruct the model to avoid every pattern it lists. Differentiate voices by format (personal vs company, interview vs demo). Add concrete metrics, numbers and personal anecdotes. Limit the model to light grammar cleanup on your own drafts.
techniques.when: Whenever captions or written posts must not read as AI-generated.

techniques.name: Weekly process-review skill
techniques.how: Ask the agent to review your whole video process, show where most time goes, and suggest repetitive tasks to turn into tools or automations. Run it weekly. Also review post performance monthly and update the skills it names. The speakers keep one large skill per tool (for example Premiere) with sub-skills for each step, so the agent can tell which stage the project is in.
techniques.when: For ongoing optimization of any repeated agent-assisted workflow, including non-content work.

tools: GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast (as named in the talk; runs on Cerebras at ~750 tokens/sec)
Coast (local screen recording, integrates with Codex CLI; transcribed as 'Coast')
Matt Palmer's at-home studio starter pack (resource)

numbers.claim: GPT-5.6 Sol Ultrafast runs at about 750 tokens per second on Cerebras; the speakers recommend it for large-file and video processing.
The speaker cites that memory retention is about 10% after three days and about 65% with a visual aid (attributed to John Medina; the speaker's own citation, not verified here).
Speakers say about 50% of YouTube performance comes from packaging (title and thumbnail), so they suggest spending about half of production time on it.
A long interview takes about a month from prep through filming and editing for one speaker.
Sony FX3 body is about $2.5K and the lens about another $2.5K. A starter Canon EOS R50 is about $300. A mic is about $60.
A design system was generated from the creator's most recent 50 Instagram videos.
Outlier slider in the speakers' YouTube research tool runs from 1x to 20x the channel's average views.

hot_takes: Packaging (title and thumbnail) deserves around half of production time, not minutes.
Swipe files are the best input for agents because references convey taste better than text descriptions.
Captions from auto-generated AI tools are always wrong and should be fixed by an agent, not accepted as-is.
Creators who only copy top-performing topics stay behind; use outlier and framework analysis instead.
The creator must stay in the driver's seat: if the content could be produced by anyone with the same tools, nobody will watch it.

relevance.why: Its process-review and telemetry-to-skills loop is a small, concrete example of SkillForge-style mining of agent activity into skill updates, but it is about content production, not infrastructure.
relevance.action: Read the 'review my process' skill example and test a weekly prompt over one month of agent-run logs to see whether it surfaces repeated, automatable steps.

relevance.why: The two-pass structure (annotate then generate checklist) and per-step sub-skills under one tool skill map onto ProsHarness skill ranking and loop checkpoints for long agent runs.
relevance.action: Try structuring one long ProsHarness workflow as one parent skill with per-stage sub-skills, so the agent can resume from the stage it is in.
